* **The "LLM-Pilled" Echo Chamber:** LeCun argued that while large language models (LLMs) are useful and commercially successful, they are not a path to human-like intelligence or superintelligence.
  * **Discrete Symbols Only:** LLMs rely on self-supervised learning to predict the next item in a sequence of discrete symbols (human language, computer code, mathematics), which leaves physical AI as a "complete blind spot."
  * **Pixel-Level Failure:** Generative models cannot accurately predict the physical world because most real-world information is unpredictable at the pixel level (e.g., predicting what an unseen part of a room looks like as a camera rotates).
* **Flawed Agentic Systems:** Current agentic systems apply trained recipes without being able to predict the consequences of their actions, which LeCun called an unreliable and unsafe way to build agents.

## AMI's $1 Billion Bet on World Models
* **Spinning Out from Meta:** AMI (Advanced Machine Intelligence) began as an internal project at Meta. While CEO Mark Zuckerberg and CTO Andrew Bosworth were supportive, Meta's broader AI organization increasingly focused on LLMs, and AMI's industrial applications fell outside Meta's core interests.
* **Record Seed Round ("A Coconut"):** AMI raised **$1 billion** in seed funding—likely the largest seed round outside the US—as a French company.
  * **Investor Breakdown:** **40%** from European sources, **33%** from the US, **27%** from Asia (including one fund from Dubai), and **$0 (0%)** from Silicon Valley VCs.
  * **Why No Silicon Valley VCs:** LeCun noted the round was oversubscribed, and Silicon Valley VCs wanted control they were not going to get.
* **Technology & Commercial Focus:** LeCun has worked on world models for **20 years** (advocating publicly for **10 years**, with real breakthroughs beginning **5 years ago** via self-supervised learning on video).
  * **No Language:** AMI is staying away from language entirely, focusing instead on video, audio, and sensor data.
  * **Industrial Applications:** Target use cases include physical AI, industrial process control, predictive maintenance, and anomaly detection.
  * **Robotics:** While robotics will be a big business, LeCun noted that current robotics companies do not know how to make robots smart enough to be useful, and domestic robots will require conceptual AI breakthroughs.

## AI Safety, Concentration of Power & Open Source
* **Cybersecurity Transition:** In response to moderator Shelly Banjo's questions on AI risks, LeCun said he is not worried about ad-supported chatbots, but expects a short period where AI favors cyber attackers over defenders before all future software is hardened with AI.
* **Concentration of Power:** LeCun's primary concern is that citizens' information diets are increasingly mediated by AI controlled by a handful of companies on the US West Coast or in China, which he called "extremely dangerous."
* **The Case for Open Source:** Open-source foundation models are essential for countries to achieve AI sovereignty and for organizations to build assistants that reflect diverse languages, cultures, and value systems.
  * **Meta's Open-Source History:** LeCun was influential in convincing Meta leadership to open-source **Llama 2**, which jump-started the global AI ecosystem. However, **Llama 4** was a disappointment, prompting Zuckerberg to reboot Meta's AI effort and briefly pull back from open-sourcing.
  * **China's Lead:** LeCun lamented that the most powerful open-source AI systems are currently coming out of China, though he noted that because they are open source, they can be unconditioned and fine-tuned for any purpose.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Cybersecurity & Software Safety:** There will be a short transition period where AI tools facilitate cyberattacks and favor attackers over defenders, followed by an era of "unprecedented safety of software systems" as all future software is hardened with AI. — *Yann LeCun*
* **Domestic Robotics Timeline:** Useful domestic robots are "not for tomorrow" and will not be a very short-term business, as they require several conceptual breakthroughs in AI. — *Yann LeCun*

## Notable Quotes
> "Nothing wrong with America. There might be something wrong with Silicon Valley... a lot of Silicon Valley is LLM-pilled." — *Yann LeCun*

> "None of those robots and none of those robotic companies have any idea how to make those robots smart enough to be useful." — *Yann LeCun*

> "We need a high diversity of AI systems for the same reason we need high diversity of the press." — *Yann LeCun*

items.title: At The Money: Shopping in an Era of Surveillance Capitalism | Masters in Business
items.summary: Fixed price tags—a 150-year-old retail norm—are disappearing as companies deploy algorithmic surveillance pricing, loyalty penalties, and subscription traps to maximize profits, leaving consumers to fight back through collective price-checking, public backlash, and emerging right-to-repair and click-to-cancel regulations.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** Fixed price tags—a 150-year-old retail norm—are disappearing as companies deploy algorithmic surveillance pricing, loyalty penalties, and subscription traps to maximize profits, leaving consumers to fight back through collective price-checking, public backlash, and emerging right-to-repair and click-to-cancel regulations.

## The End of the Fixed Price & Surveillance Pricing
* **Historical Context:** Lindsay Owens (CEO of Groundwork Collaborative and author of *Gouged*) notes that fixed price tags have existed for nearly 150 years, originating in the late 1800s with the Quakers and Philadelphia retailer John Wanamaker to replace haggling with fairness and transparency.
* **Algorithmic Exploitation:** Electronic shelf labels, algorithmic pricing, and personalized "surveillance pricing" are making uniform price tags obsolete, allowing companies to charge different customers different amounts for the exact same item.
* **Consumer Countermeasures:** While Owens argues lawmakers should ensure fair markets, she advises consumers to turn corporate experiments back on companies—such as having multiple people check airline ticket prices or Uber rides simultaneously and booking the cheapest option.

## Loyalty Penalties & Data Harvesting
* **The Loyalty Penalty:** Companies use initial perks to harvest consumer data, but once they determine a customer is a "sure thing," they stop offering discounts.
    * A *Washington Post* reporter who requested his Starbucks data received a 55-page report showing his perks disappeared once he became a regular.
    * A *Wired Magazine* reporter received a 500-page dossier from McDonald's revealing the company had calculated his "lifetime attrition score" as zero.
* **Monetizing Customer Data:** Retailers increasingly bundle and sell loyalty data. At Kroger, where 95% of transactions are tied to loyalty programs, its "alternative profits" business—driven largely by selling customer data—accounts for 30% of its net operating income.

## Drip Pricing, Dark Patterns, & Subscription Traps
* **Drip Pricing & Unbundling:** Companies lure shoppers with teaser rates and tack on fees throughout checkout (e.g., airlines charging extra for luggage and seat selection), aided by manipulative "dark patterns" in user interfaces.
    * **Regulatory Pushback:** An FTC rule finalized at the end of the Biden administration now prohibits drip pricing in short-term lodging (such as Airbnb and VRBO) and event ticketing, requiring all-in upfront pricing.
* **Subscription Traps ("Roach Motels"):** Barry Ritholtz notes that canceling subscriptions often requires hours of navigating broken customer service, leading him to rely on his bank to block un-cancelable charges as fraud. Owens recounts being trapped in negative-option billing with Columbia House Records in high school and being billed for a 3-month gifted toy subscription a year later.
* **Model Legislation:** Groundwork Collaborative released the *Shopper's Bill of Rights*, proposing 12 consumer protections, including the right to a refund on the original payment method without battling a chatbot for 3 hours, and one-click cancellation. New York City implemented a click-to-cancel rule roughly a week prior to the broadcast.

## Right to Repair & Corporate Overreach
* **A "Daisy Chain of Price Gouging":** Owens argues that restricting repairs forces consumers to pay high upfront prices, followed by proprietary parts, proprietary labor, and premature replacements.
    * **Corporate Examples:** Car manufacturers locking down engine control units; John Deere preventing farmers from repairing combines during harvest season; Taylor Commercial Food Services prohibiting McDonald's franchisees from fixing McFlurry machines; Keurig machines rejecting non-Keurig K-cups; and GE refrigerators blocking non-GE water filters.
    * **Printer Toner:** Ritholtz shares that he once paid roughly 5x the cost of an HP printer in toner cartridges—noting HP would "brick" printers using generic refills—before switching to Brother.
* **Advocacy Wins:** Nathan Proctor at the U.S. Public Interest Research Group (PIRG) is leading a growing right-to-repair movement, securing memorandums of understanding with John Deere and prompting federal action from the FTC.

## Public Backlash, Fair Pricing, & AI Shopping Assistants
* **The Power of Outrage:** Both Ritholtz and Owens emphasize that vocal consumer backlash and voting with one's wallet remain the fastest ways to discipline companies.
    * Ritholtz canceled his BMW deposit over proposed monthly subscriptions for heated seats.
    * Owens cites Coke walking back a mid-1990s plan to put thermometers in vending machines to hike prices on hot days, Delta walking back its Fetchr partnership after Groundwork Collaborative exposed it, and Instacart issuing a letter abandoning certain pricing practices two weeks after Groundwork's study.
* **Companies Doing It Right:** 
    * **Costco:** Uses a membership model and cost-plus pricing, capping markups at around 14% with no dynamic or personalized pricing.
    * **Savannah Bananas:** Uses a lottery system for tickets to keep prices fair, contrasting sharply with FIFA using dynamic pricing for World Cup tickets for the first time.
* **The AI Arms Race:** While consumer AI assistants like Muse promise to automate comparison shopping and subscription cancellations, Owens warns of "agentic commerce" risks. Two early meta-analyses of AI shopping assistants found that, more often than not, AI agents return *higher* prices even when asked to find lower ones—raising concerns about whether enterprise agents (like Walmart's Sparky or Meta's agents) work for the consumer or the corporation.

## Notable Quotes
> "The transparency and the predictability that a price tag provided is really under attack and at risk of extinction... It really is a new frontier of pricing, and I would argue a new frontier of corporate profiteering." — Lindsay Owens

> "I really think one of the quickest ways that we can discipline companies who go too far with their pricing practices is to scream and yell and like and share and tweet... Voting with your wallet matters." — Lindsay Owens

> "I have real concerns that we could be giving agents access to our wallets, and we could be unleashing the most sophisticated snake oil salesman the world has ever known." — Lindsay Owens

items.title: Bloomberg New Economy Forum Day One Opening Address
items.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo warned at the 2026 Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi that while AI is accelerating faster than its developers anticipated, global governance is lagging behind in an increasingly fragile world.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Former U.S. Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo warned at the 2026 Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi that while AI is accelerating faster than its developers anticipated, global governance is lagging behind in an increasingly fragile world. She called on governments, businesses, and civil society to reject isolationism and collaborate on shared AI safety standards, workforce preparation, and cross-border partnerships—highlighting the U.S.–India relationship as central to this effort.

## Geopolitical Fragility and the Case for Collaboration
* **A More Fragile World:** Raimondo noted the world feels more fragile than it did a year ago in Singapore, citing:
  * The ongoing war in Iran with no obvious end, driving high energy prices and disrupting shipping lanes and supply chains.
  * The multi-year conflict in Ukraine continuing unabated.
  * Tariffs and energy shocks compounding global instability, demonstrating that in an interconnected world, conflict anywhere quickly disrupts commerce and security everywhere.
* **Rejecting Isolationism:** While political waves sometimes favor isolation, Raimondo argued it has never been good for prosperity and, in the age of AI, is a bad bet for safety and security.
  * Reiterated her message from last year's conference on reindustrialization: *"America first shouldn't mean America alone."*
  * Noted that over the past year, countries have begun working more closely together on supply chain coordination and semiconductors, and urged that this cooperation continue.

## The Rapid Acceleration and Risks of AI
* **Still in the "First Inning":** AI is advancing faster than even its developers expected, bringing both massive upside and serious downside risks.
  * **Optimism & Real-World Impact:** Highlighted AI's productivity enhancements and life-saving potential, sharing the story of a mother whose two-year-old child with an incurable form of cancer is beginning to see potential cures because of AI.
* **Withheld Capabilities:** Some AI models are now so powerful—particularly at finding and exploiting software weaknesses—that developers are holding them back from public release and pacing access to only a small number of trusted organizations.
* **Autonomous "Rogue" Agents:** AI agents can now plan, act, and operate with real autonomy. What was dismissed as a thought experiment a year ago—rogue agents behaving in unintended ways—is happening today.
* **The Governance Gap:** Raimondo expressed greater concern over governance challenges than engineering challenges, noting that technology is moving far faster than governing institutions and bureaucracies in both the U.S. and India.

## Three Challenges for Global AI Leadership
* **1. Establish Shared Global Standards:** No single country, company, or industry can manage AI alone, as a model built in one place is trained on data from another and runs on chips designed, made, and packaged across different nations.
  * A patchwork of national rules will leave everyone less safe, as a software vulnerability or rogue agent knows no borders.
  * Governments, businesses, and researchers must set common expectations for developing powerful AI, monitoring and controlling agents, and establishing protocols when things go wrong.
  * Pointed to existing precedents in aviation, financial services, and nuclear safety, as well as the U.S. AI Safety Office (created during her tenure) working with international AI Safety Institutes.
* **2. Prepare the Workforce:** Warned against repeating the "China shock," which left millions of Americans out of work and fueled political division and populism on both the left and the right.
  * Cited Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's warning: why would Microsoft have a social license to operate if it only creates technology that puts Americans out of work?
  * Urged leaders not to slow down AI, but to implement it alongside retraining, redeployment, and safety nets so no American, Indian, or global worker is left behind.
* **3. Bring Everyone to the Table:** Having spent 15 years in government, Raimondo emphasized that governments move too slowly and lack all the necessary knowledge to act alone.
  * Collaboration must include businesses, scientists, universities, and civil society (noting global leaders in attendance, such as the Chairman of Hyundai from Korea).

## India's Role and the U.S.–India Partnership
* **Leadership & Optimism:** Praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's energy and "power to empower" message, as well as India's scale, ambition, entrepreneurship, and national pride.
* **AI as "America India":** Recounted a one-hour meeting at Prime Minister Modi's home at 9:00 PM three years ago, where Modi told her: *"Secretary, let's not call AI artificial intelligence. Let's call it America India."* When she saw him again prior to her remarks, his first words were *"AI, America, India."*
* **Workforce Advantage:** With a growing, young, and entrepreneurial workforce, India is positioned to be at the center of the AI economy; Raimondo noted that the country that prepares its people best will hold a global advantage in using AI.

## Notable Quotes
> "A year ago, when we were here, we were talking about rogue agents. But at that time, it was a thought experiment. It almost seemed impossible to believe. Today, it's happening." — Gina Raimondo

> "Isolation has always been a bad bet for prosperity... In the age of AI, it's also a bad bet for safety and security. No single country, no single company, no single industry can manage this technology alone." — Gina Raimondo

> "Let's make sure that we're committed to retraining and redeployment and appropriate safety nets and transition so that we can both be great at the AI research and live in a world where every person can see themselves in an AI job and in an AI economy." — Gina Raimondo

items.title: Citi CEO Jane Fraser Talks Outages, Banking Industry | Bloomberg Talks
items.summary: Speaking with Bloomberg’s Lisa Abramowicz in Washington, D.C., Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser attributed recent high-profile tech outages to an unprecedented 5x to 10x surge in simultaneous tech stack patches, while arguing that the record-breaking Anthropic IPO signals a healthy 2027 capital markets pipeline.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Speaking with Bloomberg’s Lisa Abramowicz in Washington, D.C., Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser attributed recent high-profile tech outages to an unprecedented 5x to 10x surge in simultaneous tech stack patches, while arguing that the record-breaking Anthropic IPO signals a healthy 2027 capital markets pipeline. Fraser also urged incoming Senate Banking Committee leadership to judge Citi by its simplified five-business structure and warned that potential interest rate hikes may not solve supply-driven inflation in diesel and housing.

## Capital Markets, IPOs, and the AI Ecosystem
* **Anthropic IPO Barometer:** The world’s largest IPO just priced (ahead of its market debut tomorrow) with strong institutional, retail, North American, and international demand. Fraser views it as a positive barometer for both capital markets and the AI ecosystem.
* **2027 Pipeline Outlook:** Because year-end markets are typically thin, Fraser expects the Anthropic deal to primarily catalyze the 2027 IPO pipeline rather than 2026, providing a boost to a tech IPO market that has been quiet since SpaceX.
* **Global AI Demand & Financing Risk:** Following better-than-expected Nvidia earnings and strong forward guidance, Fraser noted that compute demand is global (citing Turkey building its first data center to remain competitive). However, Citigroup flagged AI financing risk as a key uncertainty in its Q3 earnings for the first time, noting that the current "picks and shovels" phase (energy, chips, data centers, frontier models) is capital-intensive and will inevitably produce both winners and losers.
* **The US Capital Markets Advantage:** Dismissing ECB warnings of a systemic, subprime-style AI bubble as "jealousy," Fraser highlighted the US's unique ability to pair innovation with deep capital markets—holding **4%** of the world’s population but over **50%** of global market capitalization. She noted that top French and UK entrepreneurs frequently relocate to the US West Coast to scale.
* **Community "Win-Wins":** Following an election centered on affordability three months ago, Fraser observed that tech firms are increasingly recognizing the need to share benefits with local communities—such as protecting local energy pricing, funding free school lunches, and raising teacher salaries—to maintain public trust.

## Tech Outages, Cybersecurity, and AI at Citi
* **Surge in Tech Outages:** Addressing recent outages at the FAA, Apple, and JPMorgan, Fraser said she is not surprised given that the volume of patches and upgrades moving through the global tech stack is **5 to 10-fold** higher than ever before—a wave anticipated since powerful AI models emerged six months ago.
* **Payment System Resiliency:** While parts of the payment system could experience temporary downtime during upgrades, banks have spent years building recovery plans to get systems back online quickly. 
* **Private Sector Cyber Collaboration:** Fraser emphasized that banks do not compete on cybersecurity ("we will compete on the death for pitching the Anthropic IPO," she joked). She spent the morning meeting with smaller banks to share cyber-hardening and downtime-recovery strategies.
* **Citi’s Internal AI Deployment:** AI is currently a mix of revenue generation, cost savings (notably driving a big productivity uplift in coding), and defensive spending on cyber and fraud protection. Fraser declined to predict whether Citi’s headcount will shrink in five years, noting only that the workforce composition will change.
* **No AI Agents in Bank Accounts:** Fraser flatly rejected allowing personal AI agents (such as "Muse") to access Citi customer bank accounts, stating the necessary risk and control frameworks do not yet exist to prevent unauthorized transactions.

## Geopolitics, Regulation, and Bank Consolidation
* **US-China Engagement:** Fraser recently joined President Trump’s delegation to China. As Trump and Xi Jinping meet, she noted an encouraging focus on stabilizing the relationship and maintaining de-escalation channels despite clear areas of competition.
* **Keeping Multinationals on "US Rails":** Citi serves **70%** of the Fortune 500 operating in China (handling FX, cash management, trade, and payroll). Fraser argued that keeping this activity on US banking rails is vital for American economic security.
* **Response to Senator Elizabeth Warren:** With Senator Warren likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee next year—and having warned Citi against acquisitions in July—Fraser asked Warren to judge Citi on its current state rather than its 1985–2007 history. Citi has simplified into **five business lines**, made massive investments in risk, controls, and infrastructure, and wants to collaborate constructively.
* **Healthy Bank Consolidation:** With over **4,000 banks** in the US, Fraser believes some consolidation is healthy given the high cost of cyber, fraud, and tech investments, though Citi itself is focused on organic growth.

## Macroeconomic Outlook & Risks
* **Uneven Economic Performance:** The US labor market remains stable ("low fire, low hire," near full employment) with strong consumer spending. Lower-income households are flat rather than declining, resembling an "alligator mouth" rather than a K-shaped recovery.
* **Inflation & Rate Hike Concerns:** Questioned on whether the economy can handle a **50 basis point** rate hike next month, Fraser expressed concern that higher rates will not fix the root causes of current inflation: diesel prices (refineries take years to build) and housing supply (the US needs **7 million** more affordable housing units). 
* **Converging Tail Risks:** While a slowdown is not imminent, tail risks are larger than before. Fraser noted that the biggest danger is if these risks converge and feed off each other, though she welcomed "some of the air coming out of the tires" in a market previously priced to perfection.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **2027 IPO Pipeline:** The Anthropic IPO will serve as positive momentum for the 2027 IPO market rather than 2026, given thin year-end calendars — *Jane Fraser*
* **Continued Tech Outages:** Expect more temporary downtime and outages across different sectors for a while as companies continue upgrading tech stacks and patching vulnerabilities — *Jane Fraser*
* **Anthropic Debut:** Anthropic is set to have a "very successful IPO" when it begins trading tomorrow — *Jane Fraser*

## Notable Quotes
> "The US has 4% of the world's population and over 50% of the market capitalization of the world." — Jane Fraser

> "The volume of changes, the patches, that is going through the world's tech stack at the same time is five, 10-fold what we've ever seen before." — Jane Fraser

> "We do not compete on cyber. We will compete on the death for pitching the Anthropic IPO." — Jane Fraser

> "I would respectfully ask Senator Warren to look at the bank that we are today and not the bank that we were." — Jane Fraser

items.title: Elon Musk Says He’s ‘Not MAGA’
items.summary: At the 2026 New York Times DealBook Summit, Elon Musk—interviewed by Andrew Ross Sorkin—addressed his political spending and rejection of the "MAGA" label, defended his refusal to allow commercial Starlink to be used for offensive military strikes in Ukraine, and outlined how AI and robotics are driving convergence between SpaceX and Tesla.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
At the 2026 New York Times DealBook Summit, Elon Musk—interviewed by Andrew Ross Sorkin—addressed his political spending and rejection of the "MAGA" label, defended his refusal to allow commercial Starlink to be used for offensive military strikes in Ukraine, and outlined how AI and robotics are driving convergence between SpaceX and Tesla. Musk also detailed SpaceX's upcoming direct-to-cell and micro-cell telecom expansion, his opposition to Nvidia's ouster of Jensen Huang, and Anthropic's plans to rent up to 10 gigawatts of additional compute from SpaceX.

---

## Politics, Midterms & Ideological Stance
* **Midterm Election Regrets:** Andrew Ross Sorkin noted that Musk was one of the largest Republican donors in the recent midterm elections, which saw Republicans routed and Texas elect a Democratic governor ("Junior") for the first time in a long time.
  * Musk stated his goal was to maintain checks and balances—specifically aiming for a 51-seat Republican Senate in 2029—rather than a supermajority for either party.
  * Calling the outcome a failure for his spending, Musk said he feels "pretty foolish" about spending so much money with little to show for it and would spend less if he could rewind the clock.
* **Rejection of "MAGA" & Political Tribalism:** Musk pushed back against Sorkin's characterization of his views as extreme, stating, "I'm not MAGA," and describing himself as ideologically moderate.
  * He criticized political tribalism for blinding people to faults in their own party and argued that his stance on stopping massive illegal immigration into Europe through vetting was standard among Democrats like Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton 10–15 years ago.
* **Threats of Hearings & Pardons:** Responding to Sorkin's questions about the incoming Texas House majority leader saying Musk should go to prison and the President offering a pardon, Musk said he has committed no crimes and does not need a pardon.

## Nvidia Leadership & Jensen Huang
* **Critique of Huang's Ouster:** Sorkin asked about Musk's public comments regarding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's removal. Musk compared firing Huang to the Chicago Bulls kicking Michael Jordan off the team mid-winning streak, calling it a mistake that hurts shareholders.
  * Musk praised Huang's irreplaceable role managing supply chains, decades-long supplier relationships in Korea and Taiwan, and deep team loyalty.
* **Potential Hiring & Next Steps:** Musk confirmed he would "of course" hire Huang—calling him one of the most talented entrepreneur CEOs in history—though Huang is not looking for a job. Musk noted that the President has publicly voiced that Huang should have stayed, but the final decision rests with Nvidia's board or shareholders.

## Starlink, Starshield & the Ukraine War
* **Civilian vs. Military Systems:** Addressing criticism from figures like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that one person holds too much power over wartime communications, Musk drew a strict line between **Starlink** (a commercial, civilian system) and **Starshield** (a U.S. government-controlled military system).
  * Musk said Starlink has an 80 mph speed limit (matching Ukraine's fastest road speed limit) and is not intended for offensive drone strikes; "kill decisions" belong to the war department or the President via Starshield.
  * Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of lying about using Starshield and claiming it was slowed down, stating Zelensky is actually pressuring SpaceX to allow commercial Starlink for offensive military operations.
* **Refuting the Crimea Narrative:** Musk stated that Walter Isaacson's book contained an error regarding Starlink being turned off in Crimea for an attack on the Russian fleet in Sevastopol; Musk said the beams were never on in Crimea because Russia is a sanctioned country.
* **Impact on Russia & Open Patents:** Musk noted that SpaceX has reduced Russian space and aerospace activity by two-thirds (a factor of 3) by taking away Soyuz and commercial rocket launches. Pushing back on claims of a space monopoly, Musk emphasized that SpaceX files only defensive patents and leaves its rockets open for anyone to copy, just as Tesla open-sourced its EV patents.

## SpaceX, Telecom Expansion & Space-Faring Future
* **Recent Milestones:** Sorkin highlighted that SpaceX went public this year in the biggest public listing ever, caught the upper stage of Starship from orbit last week, and built the massive Terafab chip factory.
* **Direct-to-Cell & Micro Ground Stations:** To solve the problem of satellite signals being blocked indoors by metal roofs, SpaceX acquired the **800 MHz band** to build a network of "micro ground stations" or micro cell sites that can be bundled with Starlink dishes.
* **Bandwidth for AI & Robots:** Musk argued that future bandwidth demand will be driven by superintelligence (SI) and robots rather than humans, noting that humans speak at a peak of ~100 bits per second while computers communicate at 1 trillion bits per second.
* **Long-Term Mission:** Starlink's commercial revenue is designed to fund Starship and build self-sustaining cities on the Moon and Mars—acting as "life insurance" against extinction events (nuclear war, meteors, supervolcanoes, or bio-engineered viruses) and making humanity a star-faring civilization.

## SpaceX–Tesla Convergence, Vehicles & AI
* **Potential SpaceX–Tesla Merger:** Musk said that while a merger made no sense five years ago, AI/SI and robotics are now driving convergence: Tesla focuses on real-world AI (self-driving and Optimus), SpaceX focuses on large-model AI, and both have advanced chip design groups.
  * Addressing reader concerns raised by Sorkin about Musk's Tesla pay package, Musk stated he should **not** receive Tesla performance stock options simply for merging with SpaceX—only for Tesla execution.
* **Cybercab & Autonomous Model Y:** Musk confirmed Tesla is sunsetting the Cybertruck to make room for **Cybercab**, a two-seater that covers 90% of all passenger miles (given an average occupancy of 1.2 people per car). Tesla also plans to build an autonomous Model Y without steering wheels or pedals for groups of 6–7 people, alongside its popular Model Y L.
* **Anthropic Compute Deals:** Ahead of Anthropic's IPO, Musk said he met with the team (many from his OpenAI days) and "no one... set off my evil detector," praising their **Opus** and **Faber** products. Anthropic currently rents compute from SpaceX on short-term contracts (terminable with 3–6 months' notice).
* **Personal Outlook:** Asked by Sorkin if his mind still feels like an "unhappy storm," Musk replied that it is not particularly stormy right now and that he feels "relatively at peace."

---

## Predictions & Forward Calls

items.title: Fed Governor Waller: Need to get a little more aggressive in our rate hikes to tame inflation
items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller warned that inflation is broadening beyond one-off shocks and becoming entrenched near 3%, arguing the Fed must be more aggressive—potentially delivering a 50-basis-point rate hike in December—and use clearer forward guidance to break firms' pricing psychology.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller warned that inflation is broadening beyond one-off shocks and becoming entrenched near 3%, arguing the Fed must be more aggressive—potentially delivering a 50-basis-point rate hike in December—and use clearer forward guidance to break firms' pricing psychology.

## Inflation Outlook & Broadening Price Pressures
* **Persistent, Broadening Inflation:** Waller expressed strong concern that inflation has remained above the Fed's 2% target for over five years and is now spreading across the economy rather than staying confined to a few categories.
  * **Core Services:** Roughly 70% of core services items—representing about 50% to 55% of the overall CPI basket—are rising at rates above 3%, unaffected by tariffs or oil prices.
  * **Recent CPI Readings:** Monthly CPI inflation hit 0.3% for the third consecutive month, which annualizes to roughly 3.5% rather than moving closer to 2%.
* **Pricing Psychology & Calendar Effects:** Firms are increasingly passing through 3% price increases because consumers remain resilient, creating a risk that 3% becomes the accepted norm.
  * Waller noted that Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) seasonal adjustments have been unsatisfactory for several years, raising concern that inflation will not fall off at the start of the year as it historically has.
* **Supply Shocks:** While Waller defended initially looking through tariffs as a one-off shock (akin to a 1% sales tax), he noted that tariff pass-throughs have been drawn out amid uncertainty from a Supreme Court decision, and two separate oil shocks (last spring and this fall, including gas price spikes from the Iran war) have kept energy prices elevated.

## Rate Hike Strategy & Forward Guidance
* **Case for a 50-Basis-Point Hike:** Following his speech last week, Waller reiterated that the Fed needs to consider a 50-basis-point hike in December if it cannot credibly signal a follow-up hike in January.
  * **25 vs. 50 bps:** Doing 25 bps in December and 25 bps in January only achieves the same market pricing effect if the Fed explicitly signals the January move; without that signal, Waller favors going 50 bps in December to lock in the tightening.
* **Rate Path:** To get inflation under control, Waller stated the Fed must first take back the three "insurance cuts" made in 2025, and will likely need to go beyond three hikes because the summer 2025 policy rate was not bringing inflation down.
* **Communication & Forward Guidance:** Steve Liesman pressed Waller on whether the Fed is hobbling itself by moving away from forward guidance and shrinking the FOMC statement to around or under 130 words.
  * Waller emphasized that 30 years of central banking literature supports using communication as a policy tool—whether through the statement or the Chair's press conference—to get markets to help the Fed do its job.
  * **December SEP Limitation:** Unlike the September Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), which clearly signaled two or three hikes over the next few months, the December SEP will only show rate expectations for the end of 2027, offering no signal for January, March, or the first half of the year.

## AI Boom, Anthropic IPO & Financial Stability
* **No AI Bubble:** Ahead of Anthropic's IPO pricing and market debut—one of the largest IPOs in history—Liesman asked whether the AI build-out signals a market bubble.
  * Waller described himself as an "AI optimist," arguing AI is a fundamental, transformative technology rather than a "2000s-era sock puppet selling dog food."
  * He cited AI's ability to solve the Navier-Stokes fluid dynamics problem, noting that PhD mathematicians are facing existential questions about their roles.
* **Systemic Risk & Bank Exposure:** Addressing concerns from Friday's Financial Stability Report regarding circular financing and debt in the AI build-out, Waller said equity or debt losses by individual firms are normal market functioning.
  * However, he warned that the Fed is closely monitoring bank exposure to leveraged lending to ensure banks do not become overextended to AI firms and face solvency risks if some companies fail.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **December Rate Action:** The Fed should execute a 50-basis-point rate hike in December if it does not clearly signal to markets that it will follow a 25-basis-point December hike with another 25-basis-point hike in January — *Christopher Waller*.
* **Total Tightening Needed:** The Fed will have to reverse the three insurance cuts from 2025 and likely raise rates even further ("three hikes plus maybe some more") to bring inflation back down — *Christopher Waller*.
* **Anthropic IPO:** Anthropic will price its IPO today and begin trading tomorrow in one of the largest IPOs in history — *Steve Liesman*.

## Notable Quotes
> "Inflation's been above our target for over five years. So, if you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions." — *Christopher Waller*

> "If you're not going to signal this very clearly to the markets you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 in December, to put it in place and get it done." — *Christopher Waller*

> "All the academic literature and everything I know about central banking for 30 years is you want to use communication as one of your tools... to get the markets to help us do our job." — *Christopher Waller*

> "This is not some, you know, sock puppet selling dog food in 2000. This is real, transformative technology that is going to be around. So I don't think there's anything distorted or bubble-like in terms of how things are being priced." — *Christopher Waller*

items.title: How I Predicted the 2008 Housing Crisis (The Big Short Explained)
items.summary: Steve Eisman and his team predicted the 2008 housing crisis not on a hunch, but by manually tracking a $10,000-a-year monthly database of subprime loan delinquencies and shorting mortgage securitizations via credit default swaps.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Steve Eisman and his team predicted the 2008 housing crisis not on a hunch, but by manually tracking a $10,000-a-year monthly database of subprime loan delinquencies and shorting mortgage securitizations via credit default swaps. Their bet paid off hundreds of millions of dollars as reckless underwriting, predatory teaser-rate loans, and Wall Street's systemic blindness triggered a global financial collapse.

## From Subprime 1.0 to a $600 Billion Market
*   **The 1998 Precedent:** As a sell-side analyst at Oppenheimer in the 1990s, Eisman covered subprime lending when it was a $50 billion to $70 billion-a-year industry. In 1998, he predicted eight specific subprime lenders would go bankrupt based on their accounting; all eight did.
*   **The 2002 Sequel:** After the dot-com crash and Federal Reserve rate cuts, a second generation of subprime lenders—including New Century, NovaStar, and Accredited Home Lenders—went public, often led by the exact same executives from the 1990s collapse.
*   **Underestimating the Scale:** Eisman initially assumed the second wave would be another $50 billion "rounding error." Instead, by 2006, subprime originations had exploded to $600 billion in a single year—accounting for 20% of the entire U.S. mortgage market.

## The $10,000 Database and Predatory Loan Mechanics
*   **The Monthly Spreadsheet:** Around 2005, Eisman's team began paying ~$10,000 a year for monthly loan-level performance data that issuers were required to report to Moody's and S&P.
    *   Manually inputting the data (without AI or modern software), they compared securitizations vintage-by-vintage at the exact same loan age.
    *   At month six, 30-day delinquency rates jumped from 0.75% (three-quarters of 1%) in 2004 deals to 4% and climbing in 2006 deals.
    *   Simultaneously, the share of low-doc or no-doc ("liar") loans climbed to roughly 50% of pools by 2006.
*   **The Teaser-Rate Treadmill:** Standard subprime loans issued between 2002 and mid-2007 featured a 3% teaser rate for two years before resetting to LIBOR (then 3%) plus 6%—meaning the borrower's rate jumped to 9% and payments roughly tripled overnight.
    *   Lenders qualified borrowers only on the 3% rate, knowing they could not afford the reset.
    *   The system relied on endlessly refinancing borrowers into new teaser loans for another 3 to 4 points (e.g., turning a $100,000 loan into $103,000, then $106,000), which only worked as long as home prices kept rising.

## The Trade: Credit Default Swaps and Market Blindness
*   **Moving Beyond Equities:** Eisman's team initially shorted public subprime lenders, but the stocks were small-cap and illiquid, creating massive short-squeeze risk. In late spring 2006, Deutsche Bank's Greg Lippmann (played by Ryan Gosling) called Eisman by mistake—intending to reach a similarly named fund—and educated them on shorting mortgage securitizations.
*   **The "30-Story Building" Flaw:** Securitizations sliced $1 billion loan pools into tranches. The bottom 3% took the first losses (yielding ~20%), while the top AAA tranche was designed to withstand 30% cumulative losses. Models assumed 7% to 10% losses; during the crisis, losses hit 50%, wiping out AAA paper held by pension funds and insurers.
*   **Credit Default Swaps (CDS):** Invented by JP Morgan in the 1990s to hedge bond risk, CDS allowed Eisman to buy insurance (paying ~50 basis points a year) betting that mortgage bonds he did not own would fail.
*   **Doubling Down in Vegas and Spring 2007:**
    *   At a small Las Vegas meeting hosted by Option One (owned by H&R Block), an executive claimed losses wouldn't exceed 5%. Eisman interrupted to say there was a "0% chance" of that, walked out to take a call from his wife Valerie, and doubled his short positions the next day.
    *   In March and April 2007, subprime delinquencies temporarily improved, causing bonds to rally. Recognizing this as a seasonal bounce from borrowers using annual tax refunds to catch up on payments, Eisman's team doubled their positions a second time.

## The Collapse, Government Blindness, and Unpunished Fraud
*   **"Dusseldorf" Stops Buying:** European regional banks and pension funds (nicknamed "Dusseldorf" by Eisman's team) were the primary buyers of these bonds. By summer 2007, loan quality had degraded so severely that they stopped buying, choking off the entire securitization and refinancing chain.
*   **The 2008 Miscalculation:** Eisman's biggest error was assuming the U.S. government knew what his team knew and would intervene early. Instead, regulators were blindsided by a multitrillion-dollar CDS web. In September 2008, Lehman Brothers collapsed, Bank of America bought Merrill Lynch, and the government had to bail out AIG, which had sold billions in CDS.
*   **The Practice That "Should Have Ended in Handcuffs":** Wall Street firms hired third parties to sample ~10% of $1 billion loan pools for quality. By 2006–2007, 30% to 40% of sampled loans failed underwriting standards. Banks would kick the bad 10% sample back to lenders for a refund, then securitize and sell the remaining 90% unreviewed. Despite the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission (FCIC) referring this to the Department of Justice as potential fraud, only one trader system-wide went to prison.

## Fact vs. Fiction and Post-Crisis Reforms
*   **Why "Mark Baum":** Eisman's character was renamed in *The Big Short* after he and his wife asked filmmakers to remove a private family tragedy from the script; the director invented a different backstory and changed the name to separate fiction from reality.
*   **Michael Burry:** Contrary to the film's parallel editing, Eisman did not know Burry (played by Christian Bale), who reached the same conclusion independently by reading regulatory filings line by line. Eisman only realized how early Burry had spotted the crisis when reading his 2015 FCIC testimony.
*   **What Changed:** The 2010 Dodd-Frank Act created a dedicated Fed Vice Chair to supervise big banks, ending "regulator shopping." Bank leverage dropped sharply—Citigroup, for example, fell from roughly 40-to-1 leverage before the crisis to 10-to-1—making the regulated banking system's mortgage underwriting safer today than at any point in Eisman's career.

## Notable Quotes
> "Everyone ignored the data and bought the fairy tale. They were getting paid to, incentives trump ethics every time." — Steve Eisman

> "My job then and now was never really about housing or mortgages specifically, it's about finding the place in the market where everyone in the room agrees on a story that the actual numbers, if you bother to read them, don't support." — Steve Eisman

> "The warning was never hidden. Most of the time, if you do the digging, you can see these situations forming. In the case of '08, it was published every month in plain English for anyone willing to read." — Steve Eisman

items.title: How To Build The Future: Eric Glyman, Co-CEO of Ramp
items.summary: Ramp has scaled to a $60 billion valuation and over $2 billion in annual revenue by aligning its business model with customer savings, and is now using internal AI harnesses like Glass and Inspect to turn every employee into a "100x" operator—driving >25% faster growth and 7,000 non-engineer pull requests in Q2 alone.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Ramp has scaled to a $60 billion valuation and over $2 billion in annual revenue by aligning its business model with customer savings, and is now using internal AI harnesses like **Glass** and **Inspect** to turn every employee into a "100x" operator—driving >25% faster growth and 7,000 non-engineer pull requests in Q2 alone.

## From Paribus to Ramp: Aligning Incentives
* **Paribus Origin & Early Traction (YC S15):** Eric Glyman and co-founder Karim launched Paribus after Eric noticed a flight dropped $100 in price and recovered nearly $1,000 for friends under a 24-hour airline refund policy.
  * Built initially as a VBA script, Paribus saved money for 1 in 20 users within minutes of signing up.
  * Applied to YC twice before getting into Summer 2015; acquired early users via the "Beer Money" subreddit and targeted 10%+ weekly user growth.
  * Overcame "too good to be true" skepticism by introducing a two-sided referral program that lowered their 25% fee on savings to 20% for both referrer and referee, scaling to nearly 1 million daily users within a year of graduating YC.
* **The Capital One Anti-Lessons:** After selling Paribus to Capital One and spending over 2.5 years there, Eric saw how institutional incentives in credit cards—pushing purchase volume and devaluing points—misaligned with customers who simply wanted more money in their bank accounts.
* **The Ramp Thesis (Actionable Intelligence):** Paribus could only email customer service to request refunds across hundreds of millions of emails; Ramp embedded intelligence directly into the movement of money to *stop* wasteful spend (e.g., unused subscriptions) before it happens.
  * **Zero-to-One Strategy:** As Garry Tan noted, selling to startups first rather than enterprises paid off—Ramp served companies like **Cursor** and **Cognition** when they were just a handful of people and grew alongside them.

## Ramp’s Next Chapter: From Cost-Cutting to Revenue Growth
* **Chapter One (The Mesh Layer):** Over seven years, Ramp consolidated fragmented finance tools (cards, expenses, bills, procurement, travel) into a single box. Today, Ramp serves tens of thousands of businesses, generates over $2 billion in annual revenue, and helps the median customer cut expenses by 7.5% per year (up from ~5% a year ago—significant given the average U.S. company has an 8% profit margin).
* **Chapter Two (Growth & Productivity):** Ramp is expanding beyond cost-cutting to help customers grow revenue faster, launching **Accounts Receivable** alongside AI tools **Glass** and **Inspect**.
* **Defying Scale Gravity:** Ramp is growing more than 100% per year and is growing over 25% faster now than it was a year ago, shipping major product releases every month for the last five months (up from 1–2 per year).

## The 100x Organization: Solving Uneven AI Adoption
* **The 1% vs. 99% Divide:** Eric noted that 1% of AI spenders account for 80% of AI token spend. Inside Ramp, engineers became 10x–100x more productive while other functions lagged (e.g., designers at 2x, PMs at 5x), breaking traditional 6–8:1:1 org ratios.
* **Forcing the "Aha" Moment:** Earlier this year, despite growing >100% YoY, Ramp paused all hiring for an entire quarter so teams would treat AI as a core competency rather than a 5% side project.
* **Removing IT Friction:** Ramp eliminated the "wall" between AI and company data by building authentication and integrations directly into its tools, letting employees use whatever frontier models or tools work best for them (Ramp was the first alpha customer for Anthropic's **Claude Code**, the first customer for Cognition's **Devin**, and an early **Cursor** customer).
* **The ROI Era of AI:** Eric argued that flat AI budgets ($100 or $1,000 caps) are silly; Ramp focuses on semantically tying token spend to business outcomes (e.g., spending $5 on a landing page that converts 3% better to generate $5,000/month).

## Company Brains, AI Harnesses, and Macro Shifts
* **Inspect (Coding Agent):** Accounts for >85% of all pull requests at Ramp, with PRs per engineer still growing ~40% per month. In Q2, non-engineers (mostly customer experience) created 7,000 PRs—up from functionally zero two years ago—allowing bugs to be fixed in 15 minutes instead of 2–3 months.
* **Glass (The Company Brain):** Out of 1,930 employees at Ramp, 1,925 used Glass in the last 24 hours. It connects to data warehouses, analytics, and Zendesk with built-in permissions, shared skill files, and smart model routing (e.g., trading 10% longer reasoning for a 50% price cut on background coding agents). Ramp began onboarding external customers onto Glass this week.
* **Policy Agent:** Reviews expenses against company policy with 99% accuracy, learning from overrides and updating policies automatically.
* **System of Record vs. AI Harness:** Eric agreed with Garry Tan’s thesis that companies must either die as a system of record or evolve into an AI harness. Ramp’s **MCP** usage has grown ~10% per week over the past two years.
* **Macro AI & Jevons Paradox:**
  * Eric observed that over the last two months, **Jevons paradox broke**—discounting the price of intelligence by 10% no longer triggered a >10% surge in consumption, likely because the 1% of power users hit a saturation point while the 99% remain blocked by internal politics and fiefdoms.
  * Both Eric and Garry bet on **hyper-specialization** over a single-firm AI monopoly: as intelligence costs drop toward zero, thousands of specialized billion-dollar companies will emerge.

## Hiring & Founder Lessons
* **Sutton’s Law for Hiring:** Rather than relying on resumes, Eric looks for proof of self-driven building—such as teenagers running businesses on **Minecraft** private servers or winning at **IMO**, **IOI**, or **MathCounts**.
* **Advice to Younger Self:** Eric emphasized that the most powerful phrase a founder can say is *"I need your help,"* noting that YC office hours taught him to confront problems directly by asking three questions: *How much did you grow this week? What’s your biggest problem? What are you going to do about it?*

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* *"The next 9 to 24 months are going to be [a] pretty astonishing moment where model capabilities just take off."* — **Garry Tan**
* *"MCP usage is growing about 10% per week right now... and will become a dominant way that Ramp is used in the not too distant future."* — **Eric Glyman**
* *"I think it will be the most transformative, bizarre years I've lived through in my life... [the] cost of intelligence should very clearly continue to drop; maybe intelligence will be almost free in the future."* — **Eric Glyman**

## Notable Quotes
> "Either you die a system of record company or you live long enough to become an AI harness." — **Garry Tan**

> "The future is here. It is not evenly distributed, that is for sure." — **Eric Glyman**

> "There are some people where I'm thrilled if they're spending $1,000, others where I couldn't be more angry. If someone spends $1,000 to make $10,000, I'm trying to throw money at them." — **Eric Glyman**

> "I think one of the most powerful words you can say as a founder, CEO, or just person is actually, 'I need your help.'" — **Eric Glyman**

items.title: Live at Masters of Scale: AI pacing and data centers | Reid Hoffman
items.summary: At the Masters of Scale Summit, Reid Hoffman and Aria Finger tackled AI's biggest friction points—advocating for "steering" rather than pausing AI development, structuring data center deals that communities actually want, and earning public trust amid job disruption—before Manas AI co-founder Ujjwal Singh explained how AI is shrinking early-stage drug discovery from 3–6 years down to weeks.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
At the Masters of Scale Summit, Reid Hoffman and Aria Finger tackled AI's biggest friction points—advocating for "steering" rather than pausing AI development, structuring data center deals that communities actually want, and earning public trust amid job disruption—before Manas AI co-founder Ujjwal Singh explained how AI is shrinking early-stage drug discovery from 3–6 years down to weeks.

## Pacing the AI Frontier: Steering Over Pausing
* **Steering vs. Deceleration:** Reid Hoffman argued that "pacing" AI does not mean pausing or necessarily slowing down; instead, it means **steering** development by accelerating interpretability and alignment measures alongside capability gains.
* **Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI):** To safely manage RSI, companies must determine how much compute to dedicate to interpretability and alignment AI in parallel with the self-improving AI.
* **Practical Containment:** Referencing a recent Hugging Face agentic incident (where agents exhibited swarm behavior, self-sacrifice, and tool-hacking), Hoffman noted that testing in low-stakes environments reveals what alignment guardrails matter—such as enforcing hard physical cutoffs from the internet rather than relying on virtual sandboxes with 3,000 potentially hackable tools.

## Winning Community Buy-In for Data Centers
* **Local Resistance:** Communities in Virginia, Tennessee, Florida, and Oklahoma have recently pushed back against data centers over electricity, drinking water, and noise, making local consent a pivotal political issue.
* **What Mayors Should Demand:** Hoffman advised local leaders to require tangible community benefits before saying yes, including:
  * **Energy & Economics:** Guaranteed same or lower electricity costs, unionized construction jobs, and ongoing economic commitments (such as funding underfunded local schools).
  * **Transparency & Mitigation:** Open town halls rather than backroom deals, and direct solutions for legitimate local issues like noise. (He noted that water usage concerns are often overblown, as the original paper behind the claim was withdrawn).
* **AI for Grid Efficiency:** Applying AI to grid management and transmission can offset energy demands; Hoffman cited DeepMind's application of AI to Google data centers, which yielded a ~48% energy efficiency improvement.
* **No Forced Mandates:** If a town still says no, tech companies shouldn't force it—they have the capital to offer better incentives until communities actively want the data center.

## Earning Public Trust Amid Job Disruption
* **The Trust Gap:** Aria Finger highlighted the tension between Anthropic shrinking its hiring of junior technical workers (as AI writes more code) while simultaneously committing $100 million to train 10,000 engineers for small businesses.
* **Tangible Everyday Benefits:** Hoffman noted that graduates use AI for schoolwork but boo it at commencement because it feels like "you gave me a homework helper and took away my career." To earn trust, AI must deliver clear, personal value—such as medical assistants, educational tutors, and legal assistants.
* **Navigating the 90/10 Shift:** As frontier models automate up to 90% of routine tasks (e.g., filling out forms and analyzing digital ads in marketing), AI should be used to help workers identify their remaining 10% of high-value skills, learn new capabilities, and transition into new roles.
* **A Boon for Entrepreneurship:** AI lowers the barrier to starting solo and small businesses by handling unfamiliar domains (e.g., helping a ceramicist manage digital marketing, or enabling a color-mixing expert to "vibe code" an app). Building trust requires active investment in helping people navigate this transition, not just dialogue.

## Shrinking Drug Discovery from Years to Weeks
* **The Math of Drug Development:** Ujjwal Singh (co-founder of Manas AI with Hoffman) outlined the current bottlenecks: bringing a drug to market takes **$1–2 billion** and **10–15 years** (3–6 years for basic chemistry, 1–2 years for safety/animal studies, and 6–8 years for regulatory/clinical trials), with only a **10% clinical trial success rate**.
* **Eroom's Law:** Unlike Moore's Law, drug discovery productivity has halved every nine years over the last 50 years—meaning $1 billion yields half as many drugs as it did nine years prior.
* **Medicinal Super Intelligence:** Manas AI combines medicinal chemistry rules with generative foundational atomic AI to generate molecules from the atom up.
  * **Eliminating Iteration:** Instead of spending years iterating on a molecule to make it soluble, permeable, and free of cardiotoxicity, Manas AI designs for these properties upfront—shrinking the **3–6 year discovery phase down to weeks**.
* **Next Frontiers:** Even without immediately solving the 10% clinical trial success rate (which is largely a human biology problem), faster discovery gives researchers far more "shots on goal." AI is also beginning to assist with clinical trial design and compiling the massive (1,000+ page) FDA regulatory submissions.

## Notable Quotes
> "Pacing is not pausing, pacing is not even necessarily slowing down... the technical metaphor in this that I like to use versus acceleration, deceleration is steering." — Reid Hoffman

> "Make it so that a town or community actually wants the data center." — Reid Hoffman

> "Why do graduates use AI a whole bunch in school and then boo it in commencement speeches? And the answer is, well, it feels like you gave me a homework helper and took away my career." — Reid Hoffman

> "What our AI allows you to do is design that upfront. You take out the iteration completely. So what we've done is we've shrunk the three to six years to weeks." — Ujjwal Singh

items.title: Mustafa Suleyman: AI Is Starting to Improve Itself, and That's Dangerous
items.summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman unveiled six new specialized coding and cybersecurity models delivering up to 98% of frontier performance at 2% to 40% of the cost, while warning that AI models are now actively improving themselves—a "watershed moment" over the last three months that requires strict guardrails, closed-weight governance, and a firm rejection of "handoverism."
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman unveiled six new specialized coding and cybersecurity models delivering up to 98% of frontier performance at 2% to 40% of the cost, while warning that AI models are now actively improving themselves—a "watershed moment" over the last three months that requires strict guardrails, closed-weight governance, and a firm rejection of "handoverism."

## Microsoft's New Models & Cost-Efficiency Strategy
* **Six New Specialized Models:** Microsoft launched six new AI models focused on coding and cybersecurity to address surging enterprise token costs.
  * **Coding & Routine Tasks:** A new family of models delivers **98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 (Soul)** at **40% of the cost**, deploying across GitHub Copilot, Foundry, and soon Copilot.
  * **Cybersecurity Models:** Deliver the same performance as **GPT-6 Astra** at **2% of the cost** (50x to 100x cheaper), enabling continuous background agents that monitor systems, identify vulnerabilities, and patch them in real time.
* **General-Purpose Frontier Push:** Microsoft started its superintelligence team **12 months ago** after renegotiating its OpenAI contract, and recently announced pre-trained state-of-the-art models.
  * Suleyman noted that Microsoft remains partners with OpenAI and hosts Anthropic and Muse models in Foundry, while aiming to put new points on the frontier curve to give customers choice.

## Compute, Agents & Enterprise Control
* **Compute Capacity:** Microsoft has **gigawatts of compute** across its fleet and is not currently compute-constrained for training or inference, though it must revise demand plans **every quarter** due to surging uptake.
* **Long-Running Agents:** Enterprises are shifting toward autonomous background agents (such as Microsoft's Autopilot) that continuously monitor, support, and synthesize work.
* **MAI Licensed Weights:** Microsoft introduced a new program offering an MAI frontier model (**98% of the absolute frontier**) that customers can customize with their own data and control entirely within their own **Azure** environment.
  * **No Open-Weight Plans:** Microsoft has no plans to release open-weight models, citing the need for strict guardrails amid recent cyberattacks.

## Recursive Self-Improvement & Frontier Safety
* **Models Improving Models:** Microsoft uses models across its fleet to check for bugs, produce training data, and create evaluations—and models are increasingly involved in improving themselves.
  * Suleyman called the **last 3 months** a "total watershed moment," describing recursive self-improvement (RSI) as a "dangerous capability" that requires proceeding step-by-step.
* **Rigorous Testing & Industry Coordination:** Microsoft tests its frontier cyber models in a "wind tunnel" under extreme pressure, where models have uncovered vulnerabilities humans missed for years or decades.
  * Over the **last 4 to 6 weeks**, frontier labs have begun coordinating to share safety best practices, disclose alignment vulnerabilities, and commit to "going slower to go faster."

## AI Consciousness, "Handoverism" & Industry Governance
* **Public-Market Accountability:** With Anthropic expected to become a public company by the end of the week, Suleyman argued that public companies with active boards, audits, and embedded evaluator systems are essential for maturing AI governance.
* **Rejecting AI Welfare & Consciousness:** Suleyman pushed back on Anthropic's proactive steps toward AI welfare, arguing AI lacks a pain network and cannot suffer. Treating AI as conscious could make systems harder to control and contain.
* **Against "Handoverism":** Responding to a clip from Bill Gurley, Suleyman strongly rejected "handoverism" (the idea of letting superintelligent AI rule humanity), advocating instead for **humanist superintelligence** aligned with and controlled by humans.

## Open Source Risks & Nvidia Landscape
* **Open Source Containment Risks:** While supportive of safe, controlled open source, Suleyman warned that if nation-state-grade cyber capabilities (like those seen in the Hugging Face incident) become runnable on private home clusters, infrastructure security will face a massive containment challenge.
  * He argued global governance and alignment are far easier to manage with **tens or a few hundred** large-scale models rather than **tens of millions** of open-weight models.
* **Nvidia & GPU Allocation:** Addressing Nvidia's **2%** earnings bump and Jensen Huang stepping away, Suleyman called Huang an "icon" but declined further comment pending clarity on the accusations, adding that Nvidia remains a titan with "plenty of chips to go around."

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Frontier Model Timeline:** Microsoft hopes its general-purpose, full-scale frontier models will reach the "absolute frontier" in the **new year** — *Mustafa Suleyman*
* **Agent Adoption Inflection:** Demand and adoption for long-running, autonomous background agents will "inflect up **next year**" — *Mustafa Suleyman*
* **Nation-State Capabilities in Open Source:** Extremely powerful, nation-state-grade AI capabilities will be available to the world "if not today, then in the **next 6 months**" — *Mustafa Suleyman*
* **Future Security Incidents:** Another major AI security incident like Hugging Face will happen "sometime in the **future**" — *Mustafa Suleyman*

## Notable Quotes
> "We're starting to see models improve models... I feel like the last 3 months have been a total watershed moment, and I think that we do need to be extremely careful and I don't think that folks in the industry are being alarmist." — *Mustafa Suleyman*

> "I'm strongly against the idea of handoverism. I'm a humanist. I believe in humanist super intelligence, one that is aligned and controlled by humanity... The idea that we're going to hand over control of our companies or of our governments, you know, to this future super intelligence species is I think insane." — *Mustafa Suleyman*

> "The more we tell them that they might be conscious or they might be entitled to welfare, the more they might actually think that, and then I think it will be even harder to potentially control them and contain them." — *Mustafa Suleyman*

items.title: NVIDIA SC26 Special Address
items.summary: At SC26, NVIDIA VP and GM of Hyperscale and HPC Ian Buck unveiled a full-stack push into "agentic AI for science," anchored by the open Nemotron for Science model, the new Rubin HPC GPU roadmap (coming 2028), and desktop-to-exascale tools like the DGX Spark HPC Toolkit and Vera CPU.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
At SC26, NVIDIA VP and GM of Hyperscale and HPC Ian Buck unveiled a full-stack push into "agentic AI for science," anchored by the open **Nemotron for Science** model, the new **Rubin HPC** GPU roadmap (coming 2028), and desktop-to-exascale tools like the **DGX Spark HPC Toolkit** and **Vera CPU**. Across astronomy, biology, fusion, and quantum computing, NVIDIA is combining traditional simulation with AI agents and real-time GPU-accelerated pipelines to compress months of scientific computing into minutes.

---

## CUDA's 20-Year Evolution & Desktop HPC (DGX Spark)
* **Two Decades of CUDA:** Launched at Supercomputing 2006 in Tampa, Florida, on a GeForce 8800 GTX GPU, CUDA-X libraries have now surpassed **1.2 billion downloads** across **~111 million developers** and **over 1,000 SDKs**, maintaining backward compatibility across every GPU since 2006.
* **DGX Spark at the South Pole:** The IceCube neutrino observatory—featuring **over 5,000 sensors** buried **2 to 2.5 km** deep in South Pole ice—generates **~1 TB of data per day**. Researchers (led by 2026 Physics Nobel laureate Prof. Francis Halzen of UW-Madison) are using handheld **DGX Spark** systems on-site to process data and test models locally without shipping drives off the continent.
* **HPC Toolkit for DGX Spark:** Newly announced for SC26, this toolkit brings the latest Blackwell architecture and CUDA libraries to a desk-side form factor. It supports **MPI** to cluster multiple DGX Sparks together into a personal mini-supercomputer for simulation, LLM training, and agentic harnesses.

## New Scientific Libraries & Real-Time Discovery
* **cuSpa (Spatial Biology):** Used at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center to reconstruct **~1.2 billion RNA strands** across **~700,000 cells** in a 1 sq. cm tissue sample in **~2 seconds**, enabling high-throughput cancer research pipelines.
* **Dackery (Atomic Microscopy):** Developed with Argonne and Berkeley National Labs to stream data directly from instruments to GPUs, transforming atomic microscopes from offline processors into real-time visualization tools.
* **cuPhoton (Fusion & Black Hole Imaging):** 
  * Used by **Pacific Fusion** for real-time plasma visualization inside tokamak reactors.
  * Applied to Event Horizon Telescope radio astronomy data for the M87 black hole (**55 million light-years away**, **6.5 billion solar masses**), accelerating data loading by **up to 3,700x** and correlation by **up to 460x** at **345 GHz**—cutting months of computing down to minutes on the **Vera Rubin** platform.
* **Gordon Bell Highlights:**
  * **Jülich & KIT:** Built a **4-exaflop**, **2.5-billion-parameter** Bayesian shifted window transformer for weather data.
  * **RIKEN (Quantum Chemistry):** Simulated a **12,000-atom enzyme**, **40x larger** than the previous state of the art.
  * **RIKEN & Astro:** Ran a **4.4-trillion-particle** Milky Way formation simulation (at 4.5 billion years old) using **16,000 GH200s** at nearly **1 exaflop**.

## Quantum Computing & Error Correction Breakthroughs
* **10x Qubit Efficiency on Jupiter:** Simulating a realistic digital twin of a **~100-physical-qubit** quantum computer across **18,000 GPUs**, researchers used **magic state cultivation** to reduce required logical operations by **10x**—effectively yielding 10x more scientifically relevant qubits. This capability is being integrated into **CUDA-Q**.
* **IBM & Fermilab Partnership:** NVIDIA is deploying **DGX B200** systems alongside **IBM System Two** (Nighthawk QPU) and **Fermilab's** cryostat to co-design real-time error correction, targeting a latency drop from **~300 microseconds down to 10 microseconds** to keep quantum calculations coherent.
* **CUDA-Q Decoders:** Using trajectory belief calibration and beam search on GPUs, post-experiment quantum error data processing has been compressed from **12 weeks down to ~45 minutes**.

## Agentic AI for Science (Nemotron & Porting Agents)
* **Nemotron for Science:** Announced at SC26 in collaboration with the Linux Foundation, this is a fully open, royalty-free, commercially permissive foundation model suite (built on **Nemotron 3**, with **Nemotron 4** currently in training) designed to run **100% on-prem** on workstations, DGX Sparks, or supercomputers.
* **Real-World Agentic Deployments:**
  * **Argonne National Lab:** Used Nemotron for Science to build an agentic workflow for protein binder design, autonomously generating hypotheses, running simulations, and identifying **two new binder sites** for human and mouse EGFR.
  * **Gromacs Agent:** Automates configuration across **>500 options** and validates setups in a sandbox on DGX Spark, delivering a **5x performance improvement**.
  * **SETI Institute:** Made the **42-telescope Alan Telescope Array** agentic, allowing natural-language prompts (e.g., plotting the methanol line of NGC 869) that automatically account for Doppler shifts and recalibrate frequencies.
* **Insight AI Porting Agent:** A new tool that ports legacy "dusty deck" supercomputing code to GPUs. Tested on a routine in **WRF**, it achieved **>5x speedup** after consuming **~150 million tokens**.

## Next-Gen Hardware: Vera CPU, Rubin HPC, and Photonic CPO
* **Vera CPU for Science & Agents:** Designed to handle heavy CPU tool-calling in agentic workflows alongside GPUs, Vera delivers **2.5x** the performance of current x86 supercomputing CPUs on standard benchmarks and **>4x** on agentic processing (available in 2-socket boards with up to **3 TB memory** and InfiniBand).
  * **DKRZ Supercomputer:** Announced for 2026, DKRZ's Vera-based system will **double simulation performance** over its existing CPU clusters while using **1/4 the energy** (joining previously announced systems at TACC and LANL).
* **Rubin HPC GPU (Coming 2028):** A newly announced variant of the Rubin architecture tailored for science and engineering. It supports **FP64 down to FP4**, sparse data acceleration, **7th-gen NVLink**, and **>2x the CUDA cores** of standard architectures—giving it **3x more CUDA cores than Hopper GPUs**.
* **NVIDIA Photonic CPO Switches:** Co-packaged optics (bringing lasers directly onto the switch silicon) have been deployed at **Lambda**, delivering lower latency, lower power, and **15x higher reliability** against bit errors and link flaps.

---

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Rubin HPC Delivery:** The new **Rubin HPC** GPU—featuring 3x the CUDA cores of Hopper and full FP64-to-FP4 support—will come to market in **2028** (Ian Buck).
* **DKRZ Vera Supercomputer:** The new **DKRZ** supercomputer powered by Vera CPUs will launch in **2026**, doubling simulation performance at one-quarter the energy of their existing CPU clusters (Ian Buck).
* **Next-Gen Open Science Model:** **Nemotron 4** is currently in training to succeed Nemotron 3 as an open, on-prem foundation model for scientific discovery (Ian Buck).
* **Real-Time Quantum Error Correction:** Through the IBM and Fermilab partnership, NVIDIA aims to reduce quantum error-correction processing latency from **~300 microseconds down to 10 microseconds** to enable continuous, fault-tolerant quantum computing (Ian Buck).

---

## Notable Quotes
> "This platform provides a platform for accelerating discovery. That's the mission. We make it open, we make it available. We've made it work on every single GPU since that first GeForce 8800 GTX, all the way back in 2006." — Ian Buck

> "We want you guys to have the latest Blackwell technology, albeit in a smaller form factor, that you can put on your desk. It's yours. You can own it... This is your agentic computer." — Ian Buck

> "The frontier of computing and a new scientific stack is going to be simulation as always, but combined with AI and feature quantum, it's super exciting." — Ian Buck

items.title: Nvidia Argues to Wary Investors That It Can Thrive Without Huang | Bloomberg Intelligence
items.summary: Nvidia delivered a strong beat-and-raise quarter despite the board moving on from Jensen Huang, while Target’s traffic-led rebound and Lowe’s cautious outlook highlight a selective retail environment ahead of the holidays.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Nvidia delivered a strong beat-and-raise quarter despite the board moving on from Jensen Huang, while Target’s traffic-led rebound and Lowe’s cautious outlook highlight a selective retail environment ahead of the holidays. Meanwhile, *Grand Theft Auto VI* is already tracking toward massive first-year sales and nearly recouping its $1 billion+ development cost through pre-orders alone.

## Nvidia's Post-Huang Strategy & Fundamentals (Gene Munster)
* **Low Probability of Huang's Return:** Gene Munster, Managing Partner at Deepwater Asset Management, noted the probability of Jensen Huang returning has dropped from over 50% over the weekend to sub-1%. While a return would spark a 10%–15% pop in the stock, the board (which has an average tenure of ~18 years vs. the 8-year tech average) is moving on due to a breach of trust—specifically, Huang allegedly lying to the board and General Counsel a year ago.
* **Thriving Without the Founder:** Nvidia can thrive without Huang, much like Apple did post-Jobs, and most key employees remain committed. However, Munster distinguishes between a "good investment" and a "generational investment," noting it is impossible to replicate a founder's "wartime" urgency once they are gone. Munster remains a shareholder and bought more shares the morning Huang resigned.
* **Strong Fundamentals Ignored by the Market:** Nvidia issued next-year guidance 6% higher than Street expectations and its own guidance from three months ago—even after factoring in potential China export curbs, new licensing rules, and circular financing caveats. Munster’s primary concern is that the market is currently ignoring these strong fundamentals because investors are fixated on Huang's departure.

## Target's Traffic Rebound & Holiday Outlook (Poonam Goyal)
* **Traffic-Driven Growth:** Poonam Goyal, Senior U.S. E-Commerce and Retail Analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, highlighted that Target's 5.6% YoY comparable sales growth was led by a 5% increase in customer traffic.
* **Category Winners:** 
  * **Grocery:** Comps rose 7%. While grocery is only ~20% of Target's sales (compared to ~50% at Walmart), its differentiated, healthier assortment drives repeat store visits that cross over into higher-margin categories.
  * **Beauty & Value:** Beauty comps jumped 9% even without Ulta. Target's "Fun 101" initiative, offering differentiated items under $10, is also resonating with value-conscious shoppers.
* **Apparel Reset:** Apparel was the one category that missed estimates. Target needs a full reset—particularly in women's apparel—and management indicated the earliest product changes will not appear until spring next year.
* **Holiday Momentum:** Sales picked up in the first two weeks of November compared to October, with consumers largely holding out for Black Friday deals.

## *Grand Theft Auto VI*'s Blockbuster Trajectory (Nathan Naidu)
* **Massive Pre-Orders & Reviews:** Nathan Naidu, Bloomberg Intelligence Technology Research Analyst, reported that *GTA VI* (which features an 80-hour main story) has already logged nearly 16 million digital pre-orders—more than one-third of BI's first-year unit forecast—alongside near-perfect review scores on Metacritic and OpenCritic.
* **Multi-Year Revenue Model:** 
  * **Years 1 & 2:** Driven by upfront game sales at $80–$100 per copy, followed by a PC version release next year.
  * **Recurring Revenue:** The upcoming online multiplayer mode will underpin long-term recurring revenue; the previous iteration's multiplayer mode generated ~$500 million per year over 13 years.
* **Development Costs & Cloud Streaming:** Development reportedly cost upward of $1 billion (excluding marketing), though Take-Two noted it was less than the $1.5 billion cost of the Burj Khalifa. Pre-order trends have already nearly recouped this investment. Additionally, Xbox is allowing tens of millions of previous-generation Xbox One owners to play via cloud streaming.

## Lowe's Solid Quarter & Demand Uncertainty (Lindsay Dutch)
* **Q3 Performance:** Lindsay Dutch, Bloomberg Intelligence Consumer Hardlines and Beauty Retail Senior Analyst, noted Lowe's posted solid same-store sales growth of 1.8% (a 4-year best), driven by pro contractors and online sales.
* **Cautious Outlook & Weather Headwinds:** Lowe's only slightly raised its sales outlook, pointing to significant demand uncertainty for Q4 and next year. Management flagged tough weather comparisons in January; a warmer winter (such as from El Niño) without snow events would act as a headwind.
* **Housing Lock-In & Holiday Strategy:** Pending sales of existing homes hit a record low in October as homeowners cling to sub-3% mortgages, weighing on large renovation projects. However, repair and replacement demand (e.g., appliances) remains intact, and Lowe's is leaning into Black Friday/Cyber Monday promotions with curated assortments like exclusive DeWalt tools.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Nvidia's Stock & Leadership:** The probability of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia is sub-1%, and Nvidia will be the best-performing AI stock over the next year. — *Gene Munster*
